title: Bathing before prayer
hook: washing the body before prayer, as the Gursikh routine describes
tomorrow: how much prayer fits into a morning that's already running late?

segments.voice: Yesterday, amrit vela: the early hour, kept for the Name before the world rushes in. Right after waking, Guru Ram Das names the next thing.

Water on skin does something nothing else does. The first cold splash at the sink, the hot shower after a long day, rain you didn't plan for: the body wakes up all at once. In the Sikh morning, water comes right after the alarm. Guru Ram Das, on ang 305, puts it in one line with the early hour: rise early, make the effort, bathe, and dip in the pool of nectar.
screen: `A COLD SPLASH, A HOT SHOWER.` → `WATER RIGHT AFTER THE ALARM.` → `ANG 305: RISE, BATHE, THE NAME.`

segments.voice: The word is ishnaan, bathing. It's plain and physical: Sikhs who keep the morning routine wash the whole body before the banis, and keep the hair clean and combed under the turban or scarf. But listen to how Guru Nanak talks about water in Japji's twentieth pauri. In paraphrase: when the hands, feet and body are dirty, water washes the dust away. When clothes are soiled, soap washes them clean. When the mind is stained with wrongdoing, it's washed by love of the Name. Two washings, one after the other. Water for the body; the Name for the mind. And the next pauri pushes further. Pilgrimages, austerities, charity earn only a sesame seed of honor, it says in paraphrase; the one who hears, trusts and loves bathes at the shrine within. So the bath at dawn isn't a ritual that cleans you for God. It's a body getting ready to sit still, while the real washing happens inside. Clean body, clear mind: the first is the doorway to the second.
screen: `ISHNAAN: BATHING.` · `JAPJI 20: WATER FOR THE BODY.` · `THE NAME WASHES THE MIND.` · `JAPJI 21: THE SHRINE WITHIN.` · then, large: `CLEAN BODY, CLEAR MIND.`

segments.voice: Go to the nearest sink, or wait for your next one, and wash your hands slowly: cool water over the backs, the palms, the wrists. Feel the water on your skin and notice it leaving. Then sit with dry hands, and let the quiet do the other washing.
Ishnaan. Bathing: water for the body at dawn, and, in Japji, the Name washing the mind.
Your line: clean body, clear mind. One washing opens the door to the other. Day done.
